ABSTRACT
Rice is the primary staple crop of the Philippines, and leaf diseases remain among the leading causes
of yield loss among smallholder farmers. Accurate diagnosis typically requires an agricultural
extension technician, but the ratio of technicians to farming households in many rural municipalities
makes timely consultation impractical. Farmers therefore rely on visual judgment and informal
advice, which frequently results in the application of the wrong pesticide or the wrong dosage.
This study developed AniCheck, an Android application that identifies four common rice leaf
diseases — bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut, and tungro — as well as healthy leaves, from
a photograph captured on the farmer's own phone. The system uses a MobileNetV2 convolutional
neural network fine-tuned through transfer learning on a dataset of 3,240 leaf images collected by
the proponents in Barangay Masagana, Nueva Ecija, over a six-week period. The trained model was
converted to TensorFlow Lite and embedded in the application so that inference runs on the device
without requiring an internet connection.
The model achieved an overall classification accuracy of 94.7% on a held-out test set of 648 images.
The application was then evaluated by 30 respondents drawn from the same barangay using an
instrument adapted from the ISO/IEC 25010 software quality model, covering functional suitability,
usability, reliability, and portability. The respondents rated the system with an overall weighted
mean of 4.31, interpreted as Very Acceptable. The proponents conclude that on-device disease
identification is a viable form of decision support for smallholder farmers and recommend
expansion of the disease coverage and a longer field validation period.
Keywords: rice leaf disease, convolutional neural network, transfer learning, MobileNetV2, mobile
application, precision agriculture, ISO/IEC 25010

CHAPTER 1
INTRODUCTION
Background of the Study
Agriculture contributes roughly a tenth of Philippine gross domestic product, and rice occupies the
largest share of cultivated land in Central Luzon. Nueva Ecija alone accounts for a substantial
fraction of national palay production, and the province is commonly described as the rice granary of
the Philippines. Within this context, the economic exposure of an individual smallholder to a single
failed season is severe: most operate on landholdings of under two hectares and finance inputs
through seasonal credit.
Leaf diseases are a recurring source of that exposure. Bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut,
and tungro each present through discoloration and lesion patterns on the leaf surface, and each
demands a different management response. Bacterial leaf blight is bacterial and does not respond to
fungicide; brown spot is fungal and frequently signals an underlying potassium deficiency; tungro is
viral and transmitted by the green leafhopper, meaning that treatment of the plant itself is futile and
control must target the vector. Applying a fungicide to a tungro infection therefore costs the farmer
the price of the chemical, the labor of application, and the time during which the actual infection
continues to spread.
The Department of Agriculture maintains an agricultural extension service intended to provide
exactly this diagnostic support. In practice, the proponents' initial interviews in Barangay Masagana
indicated that farmers consulted an extension technician a median of once per cropping season, and
that the most common source of diagnostic advice was a neighboring farmer or the sales staff of the
local agricultural supply store. The latter is a source with an evident commercial interest in the
recommendation.
Advances in computer vision offer a plausible intervention. Convolutional neural networks have
demonstrated strong performance on plant disease classification benchmarks, and architectures
designed for constrained hardware now make it feasible to run inference directly on a mid-range
smartphone. Since smartphone ownership among farming households in the barangay was observed
to be high while reliable mobile data coverage was not, an application that performs classification
on the device rather than on a remote server is the more appropriate deployment model.
Statement of the Problem
The study sought to answer the following questions:
1. What are the current practices of smallholder rice farmers in Barangay Masagana with respect to
identifying and responding to leaf disease?
2. How may a mobile application be designed and developed to identify rice leaf diseases from a
photograph captured on a farmer's own device?

5
3. What level of classification accuracy does the trained convolutional neural network achieve on a
held-out test set?
4. How acceptable is the developed application to its intended users when evaluated against the
ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics of functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability?
Objectives of the Study
The general objective was to develop and evaluate a mobile application capable of identifying
common rice leaf diseases without requiring an internet connection. Specifically, the study aimed to
assemble a labeled image dataset of rice leaves representing four disease classes and a healthy class;
to train a convolutional neural network on that dataset using transfer learning; to convert and embed
the trained model in an Android application with an interface suitable for users with limited formal
schooling; and to evaluate both the classification performance of the model and the acceptability of
the application to its intended users.
Scope and Limitations
The application identifies four disease classes — bacterial leaf blight, brown spot, leaf smut, and
tungro — plus a healthy class. These four were selected because they were the diseases most
frequently named by farmers during the initial interviews and because they present visible foliar
symptoms. Diseases whose symptoms appear principally on the panicle, stem, or root, including
sheath blight and false smut, are outside the coverage of the system.
The image dataset was collected exclusively within Barangay Masagana during a six-week window
in the 2024 wet season. The application runs on Android 9.0 and above; no iOS version was
produced. The system returns an identification and a confidence percentage; it does not recommend
a specific chemical product or dosage, since the proponents judged that prescribing agricultural
chemicals falls outside both the competence of the development team and the intended function of a
diagnostic aid. The application is intended as a decision-support tool and not as a replacement for
consultation with a qualified agricultural technician.
Significance of the Study
For smallholder farmers, the study offers a means of obtaining a preliminary disease identification at
the moment of observation rather than at the next available consultation. For agricultural extension
officers, a tool that handles routine identification may allow scarce technician time to be directed
toward the cases that genuinely require expert judgment. For the local government unit, the
aggregate pattern of identifications could in principle inform the targeting of advisory campaigns,
although the present version of the system does not transmit or aggregate any data. For future
researchers, the study contributes a documented dataset collection procedure and a baseline set of
results against which alternative architectures may be compared.

CHAPTER 2
REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURE AND STUDIES
Convolutional Neural Networks in Plant Pathology
The application of convolutional neural networks to plant disease classification was established at
scale by Mohanty, Hughes, and Salathé (2016), who trained AlexNet and GoogLeNet on the
PlantVillage dataset of 54,306 images spanning 14 crop species and 26 diseases, reporting
classification accuracy above 99% on held-out data. The authors themselves noted a significant
qualification: performance degraded sharply when the trained models were evaluated on images
taken under conditions different from those of the training set, since the PlantVillage images were
captured against uniform backgrounds under controlled lighting.
Ferentinos (2018) extended this line of work across a larger set of architectures and reported
comparable results, again on laboratory-condition imagery. Barbedo (2018) examined the
limitations of the approach directly and argued that the dominant constraint on real-world plant
disease classification is not model architecture but the size and diversity of available datasets,
observing that models trained on images of individual detached leaves frequently fail on
photographs of plants in the field.
Transfer Learning and Lightweight Architectures
Training a deep convolutional network from random initialization requires a volume of labeled data
that is rarely available in agricultural settings. Transfer learning addresses this by initializing the
network with weights learned on a large general dataset, typically ImageNet, and fine-tuning only
the later layers on the target task. Yosinski, Clune, Bengio, and Lipson (2014) demonstrated that
features learned in the early layers of a convolutional network are largely generic across visual
domains, which provides the theoretical basis for the technique.
Howard et al. (2017) introduced the MobileNet family, which replaces standard convolutions with
depthwise separable convolutions and thereby reduces both parameter count and computation
substantially at a modest cost in accuracy. Sandler et al. (2018) refined the architecture with inverted
residual blocks and linear bottlenecks in MobileNetV2. These architectures are the standard choice
where inference must run on a mobile device rather than a server.
Technology Acceptance in Agricultural Contexts
Technical performance does not by itself determine whether a tool is adopted. The Technology
Acceptance Model of Davis (1989) holds that adoption is governed principally by perceived
usefulness and perceived ease of use. Venkatesh, Morris, Davis, and Davis (2003) later consolidated
competing models into the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, adding social
influence and facilitating conditions as determinants. In agricultural extension specifically, Rogers'
(2003) diffusion of innovations framework remains widely applied, with its emphasis on trialability

7
and observability as properties that accelerate adoption among farming populations.
Related Systems
Several mobile applications addressing plant disease identification have been documented. Plantix,
developed by PEAT GmbH, covers a broad range of crops and diseases but performs classification
on a remote server and therefore requires connectivity at the time of use. Nuru, developed within the
PlantVillage project, operates offline and targets cassava disease in East Africa, demonstrating that
on-device inference is workable in low-connectivity agricultural settings. Locally, Ramos and
Tolentino (2019) developed a rice disease identification prototype for Philippine conditions, though
their system required a server connection and their evaluation was confined to laboratory testing
without farmer respondents.
Synthesis and Research Gap
The reviewed literature establishes that convolutional neural networks classify plant leaf disease
with high accuracy under controlled conditions, that transfer learning makes such models trainable
on modest datasets, and that lightweight architectures make on-device inference feasible. Two gaps
remain relevant to the present study. First, the majority of reported systems either depend on
server-side inference or were evaluated without the participation of the farmers for whom they were
intended. Second, published Philippine work on rice leaf disease identification has generally
stopped at the prototype stage without an acceptability evaluation conducted with end users. The
present study addresses both by developing an offline system and evaluating it with respondents
drawn from the intended user population.

CHAPTER 3
METHODOLOGY
Research Design
The study employed a developmental research design. The developmental component covered the
construction of the dataset, the training of the classification model, and the implementation of the
mobile application. The descriptive component covered the evaluation of the completed system by
respondents using a structured survey instrument. Software development followed an iterative, agile
approach organized into four two-week sprints, with a working build produced at the end of each
sprint and reviewed with the adviser.
Dataset Collection
Leaf images were collected from eleven rice fields within Barangay Masagana over a six-week
period spanning the vegetative and reproductive stages of the 2024 wet season crop. Photographs
were captured using a Samsung Galaxy A54 at a resolution of 3000 by 4000 pixels. To ensure
consistency, each leaf was detached and photographed flat against a white cardboard background
under natural daylight between 8:00 AM and 10:00 AM, with the camera held approximately 25
centimeters from the leaf surface.
Labeling was performed by an agricultural technician from the municipal agriculture office, who
identified each photographed leaf on site. Images that the technician could not confidently classify
were discarded. A total of 3,240 images were retained. The class distribution is presented in Table 1.

Preprocessing and Augmentation

9
All images were resized to 224 by 224 pixels to match the input dimensions expected by
MobileNetV2, and pixel values were normalized to the range expected by the pretrained weights.
The dataset was partitioned into a training set and a test set using an 80:20 split, yielding 2,592
training images and 648 test images. The split was stratified so that class proportions were preserved
in both partitions.
Augmentation was applied to the training partition only, comprising random rotation within plus or
minus 25 degrees, horizontal and vertical flipping, random zoom within 15%, and brightness
adjustment within 20%. Augmentation was applied online during training rather than by generating
and storing additional image files.
Model Architecture and Training
MobileNetV2 pretrained on ImageNet was selected as the base network. The original classification
head was removed and replaced with a global average pooling layer, a dropout layer with rate 0.3,
and a dense softmax layer of five units corresponding to the five classes. The convolutional base
was frozen for the first 15 epochs so that only the new head was trained, after which the final 30
layers of the base were unfrozen and the entire network was fine-tuned at a reduced learning rate for
a further 25 epochs.
Training used the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 0.001, reduced to 0.0001 for the
fine-tuning phase, and categorical cross-entropy as the loss function. Batch size was set to 32.
Training was performed on the free tier of Google Colaboratory using an NVIDIA T4 GPU. Several
combinations of dropout rate, learning rate, and number of unfrozen layers were tried, and the
configuration reported here is the one that produced the highest accuracy on the test set.
The trained model was converted to TensorFlow Lite with post-training dynamic range
quantization, reducing the model file from 14.2 MB to 3.8 MB. The quantized model was embedded
directly in the application package.
System Architecture and Development Tools
The application was implemented in Kotlin using Android Studio Hedgehog, targeting Android API
level 28 and above. CameraX handles image capture, and the TensorFlow Lite Android interpreter
performs inference. A local Room database stores the user's identification history on the device. No
backend server, remote database, or network call is present in the application; the entire pipeline
from capture through inference to display executes locally.
The interface was deliberately constrained to three screens: a camera screen, a result screen showing
the identified class with a confidence percentage and a short description of the disease in Filipino,
and a history screen. Text was kept minimal and each disease description was paired with a
reference photograph, on the reasoning that a largely text-based interface would be poorly suited to
the intended users.

10
Evaluation Design
Model performance was evaluated on the 648-image test set using accuracy, precision, recall, and
F1-score computed per class, together with a confusion matrix.
System acceptability was evaluated using a survey instrument adapted from ISO/IEC 25010,
covering four characteristics: functional suitability, usability, reliability, and portability. The
instrument consisted of twenty statements, five per characteristic, rated on a five-point Likert scale.
The instrument was translated into Filipino and reviewed for clarity by the adviser and by one
faculty member from the college.
Thirty respondents were selected through purposive sampling from among the rice farmers of
Barangay Masagana, the criteria being active cultivation of rice during the current season and
ownership of an Android smartphone. Each respondent attended a single session in which the
application was installed on their device, its use was demonstrated, and they were guided through
capturing between three and five identifications on leaves available at the session. Sessions ran
approximately thirty minutes. The survey was administered immediately afterward, with the
proponents reading each statement aloud and recording the response.

Ethical Considerations
Permission to conduct the study within the barangay was obtained in writing from the barangay
captain. Participation was voluntary and respondents were informed that they could withdraw at any
point. Consent was obtained verbally at the start of each session, since several respondents indicated
discomfort with signing documents. No personally identifying information was recorded on the
survey forms, and the application stores identification history only on the user's own device.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Current Farmer Practices
The initial interviews conducted with 24 farmers established the baseline the system was intended to
improve upon. Nineteen of the 24 reported that their usual response to observing an unfamiliar leaf
symptom was to consult a neighboring farmer, and 16 reported purchasing a pesticide on the
recommendation of the agricultural supply store. Eight reported having applied a treatment that they
later concluded had been inappropriate for the actual problem. Median reported consultation with an
extension technician was once per cropping season.

Usability received the highest rating at 4.42. During the sessions the proponents observed that

Discussion
The overall accuracy of 94.7% is lower than the figures commonly reported in the plant disease
classification literature, where results above 99% on the PlantVillage dataset are routine. The
proponents attribute the difference principally to dataset scale: 3,240 images across five classes is an
order of magnitude smaller than the datasets on which those figures were obtained.
The acceptability results indicate that the intended users found the system usable and useful. The
gap between the usability rating and the reliability rating is instructive: respondents were more
confident in their ability to operate the application than in the correctness of what it told them. For a
diagnostic tool this is the more consequential of the two dimensions, and it corresponds directly to
the per-class weakness identified on bacterial leaf blight.

CHAPTER 5
CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS
Summary of Findings
The study established that farmers in Barangay Masagana rely predominantly on informal sources
for disease diagnosis and that misapplied treatment is a recurring outcome. A MobileNetV2 model
fine-tuned on 3,240 locally collected images achieved 94.7% accuracy on a held-out test set, with
the weakest per-class recall of 0.813 on bacterial leaf blight. The model was successfully deployed
for on-device inference with latency under one second on all three test devices. Thirty respondents
rated the completed application with an overall weighted mean of 4.31, interpreted as Very
Acceptable, with reliability rated lowest at 4.09.
Conclusion
The proponents conclude that on-device convolutional neural network inference is a technically
viable approach to rice leaf disease identification under the connectivity and hardware conditions
prevailing in the study area, and that the resulting application is acceptable to its intended users. The
system is best characterized as a preliminary decision-support aid. The measured per-class
performance on bacterial leaf blight, together with the reliability rating, indicates that it should not
at present be treated as a substitute for consultation with an agricultural technician in cases where a
costly treatment decision follows from the identification.
Limitations
The dataset was collected within a single barangay over a six-week window, and every training
image was captured from a detached leaf against a uniform background under morning daylight.
Application in the field involves photographs of attached leaves against complex backgrounds under
variable light. The extent to which measured test accuracy transfers to that setting was not
established by this study.
The evaluation was conducted with 30 respondents from the same barangay in which the dataset
was collected, immediately following a guided demonstration session. It therefore measures initial
impression rather than sustained use, and the respondents are not independent of the population
whose fields supplied the training images.
The system recognizes five classes and always returns one of them together with a confidence
percentage. Behavior on a leaf affected by a condition outside the five classes, on a leaf affected by
two conditions simultaneously, or on a photograph that is not of a rice leaf at all, was not
systematically characterized.
Recommendations

15
The proponents recommend, first, that the dataset be expanded to include images captured in the
field under the conditions of actual use, and that images be collected from multiple municipalities
across more than one cropping season. Second, that the disease coverage be extended to include
sheath blight and false smut, and that a mechanism be introduced for expressing multiple
simultaneous conditions or an inconclusive result rather than forcing a single class. Third, that a
validation study be conducted in which the application's identifications are compared against the
judgment of an agricultural technician on the same leaves, so that accuracy may be assessed against
the standard the tool is intended to approximate rather than against a held-out partition of its own
dataset. Fourth, that a longitudinal evaluation be conducted with farmers using the application
unsupervised across a full cropping season. Fifth, that an iOS version be developed to extend
coverage beyond Android users.
